items.title: Ghana secures $4.5m Korean support to protect forts and castles from climate change
items.description: Ghana has secured a $4.5 million initiative from the Korean Government to strengthen the country’s capacity to protect its forts and castles from the growing impacts of climate change. The five-year Korea-Ghana Heritage Project on Climate Change Impact on Forts and Castles of Ghana World Heritage Property will run from 2026 to 2030. Minister of Tourism, Arts and Culture, Abla Dzifa Gomashie, announced the initiative on Monday, August 10, when she took her turn at the Government Accountability Series. She said the project had become necessary as Ghana’s coastal heritage sites face increasing threats from climate change, including coastal erosion, flooding, salt-induced deterioration, structural instability and extreme weather conditions. The initiative will initially focus on six heritage sites in the Greater Accra Region: Ussher Fort and James Fort in Jamestown, Christiansborg Castle in Osu, Fort Augustaborg in Teshie, Fort Vernon in Prampram, and Fort Fredensborg at Old Ningo. According to the Minister, the project aligns with the UNESCO World Heritage Climate Action Policy, the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDGs 11 and 13, as well as recommendations of the World Heritage Committee. She said the initiative would establish a scientific climate-risk assessment and monitoring system for the selected heritage sites while developing national and site-level policies to guide climate-responsive heritage conservation. It will also seek to strengthen the institutional and technical capacity of agencies responsible for heritage management, develop integrated data systems and climate-risk mapping, and promote greater participation by local communities and other stakeholders. The project is expected to involve government institutions, technical agencies, local communities, academia and international partners. Ms Gomashie said Ghana had already begun benefiting from capacity-building opportunities under the initiative. “Six experts drawn from various stakeholder organisations have received two weeks intensive training in climate change response policy for forts and castles in South Korea,” she said. She added that six site managers would undergo two months of training in site management in South Korea between October and November 2026, with additional training and skills development opportunities expected throughout the five-year project. The Minister said the initiative would also strengthen Ghana’s contribution to regional and international discussions on climate and heritage conservation. The project will officially be launched on August 26, 2026, at the forecourt of the Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture. The launch will be attended by Ghanaian officials and counterparts from the Korean Commission for UNESCO and the Ghana Commission for UNESCO.

items.title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
items.description: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way. But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life. Two days later, his car was found overturned – he had been shot dead while driving. Now seven members of South Africa’s special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges. There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army’s special forces, and one of them has been promoted. The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men. The case has caused consternation in one of Africa’s most robust democracies, with fears the country’s military is significantly overreaching its mandate. We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa’s killing. It did not respond. Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa – who worked for an elite police unit known as “The Hawks”. We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation – South Africa’s former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa’s commanding officer; and Mathipa’s family – to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective’s death. It presents a compelling case that South Africa’s special forces are responsible for his murder. In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting. One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers – the case that Mathipa had been investigating. After Mathipa’s death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. “You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them,” said the warning, according to police. The case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive. It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017. Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset – but had “gone rogue”, according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks. Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg’s Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government. We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga’s return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond. Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 – who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia. Court documents show that after Abadigga’s abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia. The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC’s question on whether Abadigga’s phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga’s alleged abduction. We also asked South Africa’s President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment. When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence. He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga’s brother, Ameen – who had opened a missing person’s case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police. He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg. The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do. The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers’ vehicles are clearly visible. The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces – Ameen and the IO were to discover. At the time of Abadigga’s disappearance, PCT’s directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment. Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military. So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga’s brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court. Responding to Ameen’s legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise. They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them. Domestic operations by South Africa’s military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency. We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa – Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment. When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved. When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered – according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer. “When [Mathipa] left my office he said: ‘Brigadier, you know, these people – they are going to kill me. I’m going to die’,” she told the BBC. On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective – according to Mathipa’s daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time. Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria. When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway. He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police. And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi. This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga’s disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add. New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa’s death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police’s Criminal Intelligence division. Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, “we will kill all of them”. Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa’s special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo – both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case. The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction. All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody. Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa’s murder, and Abotese’s abduction and murder. The military has refused to hand them over. In July, their lawyers cited mental health treatment for their absence. Three years after Mathipa’s killing, no trial date has been set. Meanwhile, Abadigga’s body has never been found. “[Mathipa] was barking up the right tree. He was taking on the right lion,” Vreugdenburg says of the late detective. Mathipa’s daughter Basetsana puts it starkly: “We need justice. I’m never going to see my dad anymore… Why my dad? Because he was doing his job.”

items.title: Former Thai MP allegedly kills official and confesses on YouTube
items.description: A former Thai MP allegedly shot dead a local official in the southern province of Nonthaburi, then dialled into a YouTube livestream to inform the host – a political pundit – of what he had done. Former Nonthaburi MP Chalong Reawraeng told the shocked host, Anchalee Paireerak, that he had shot Thongchai Yenprasert, a former police official, outside Thongchai’s office. Thongchai, who was hit in the neck, died in hospital. His driver was shot in the arm and hand. Chalong was arrested but then allowed to hold a press conference at a police station where he attempted to explain what had happened while smoking a cigarette. He told the reporters there that Thongchai was “angry” at him, but did not explain why. He also said he did not intend to shoot Thongchai, whom he described as a “good friend”. Chalong said he told Thongchai that he wanted to talk to him. According to local media reports, the two were involved in a personal dispute. “He [Thongchai] then pushed me, saying ‘I don’t want to talk, I don’t want to talk.'” Chalong said he then followed Thongchai towards his car. “When I pulled the gun out, I didn’t intend to shoot him. But then [Thongchai’s driver] pulled his gun out and pointed it at me, so I fired.” Thongchai, a retired police colonel, was president of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organisation or PAO, a local government body. Earlier, Chalong had called political commentator Anchalee Paireerak, who was livestreaming on YouTube at the time, to confess to the incident. Anchalee was filmed picking up a call midway through her programme. “I’ll call you back… Oh, something big [happened]? Go ahead, what’s that?” she said. Viewers could not hear what the caller said next, but Anchalee was seen reacting in shock. “Did he die? Did he die? You shot him in the head? You need to wait there for the cops,” she said on the video, which was seen by the BBC. “Don’t go anywhere.” Monday’s shooting came three days after a 14-year-old boy shot dead eight people at his home and school, then killed himself, in Thailand’s worst mass shooting since 2022. The two attacks are not related. The latest shooting will further spur debate about gun control in Thailand, which has the highest rate of gun ownership in South East Asia by a wide margin. After Friday’s school shooting, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul ordered tougher enforcement of gun laws and said police would set up checkpoints as part of a crackdown. Other measures would include tightening controls on the possession, carrying and use of firearms.

items.title: Sindh govt defers judicial commission decision on Mir Raza Ali murder case probe
items.description: Sindh Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar said on Monday the provincial government had deferred the decision on the formation of a judicial commission to probe the Mir Raza Ali murder case. Lanjar made the announcement on X, saying that Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab had spoken to Ali’s family, who had expressed “confidence in the new police team” constituted to investigate the case and was of the view that it should conduct the probe. “Therefore, the decision of establishing a judicial commission has been deferred for the time being,” the home minister said. Owner of eatery Wafflix, Ali had gone missing on July 28, and his body was found a day later with a gunshot wound in bushes in Karachi’s Gulistan-i-Jauhar. While his family was convinced that he was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, police had previously been building the case around the possibility that he died by suicide. A murder charge was eventually added to the first information report after the exhumation and a second postmortem of Ali’s body revealed that he had suffered multiple injuries and was shot in the back, ruling out the possibility of suicide. Controversy fueled by ‘miscommunication’ Sindh Inspector General of Police (IGP) Javed Alam Odho said that the investigation into the murder should be conducted in a better manner, expressing hope that the new investigation team would consider all available evidence. Speaking to the media in Sukkur, he said the government, public and police were all concerned about the case and stressed the need to examine it “with an open mind and open heart”. He said action had been taken against officers found guilty of misconduct and negligence during the investigation. IG Odho said the controversy surrounding Ali’s murder had been fuelled by “miscommunication”. “I have strictly instructed the entire investigation team to keep communication open and transparent this time, whether with the deceased’s family or the media,” he said. On Sunday, PPP leader Faryal Talpur recommended a judicial commission to probe the case, saying it should examine all aspects of the incident and bring the facts to light. A few hours after Talpur’s statement, Lanjar and Wahab had reached Ali’s residence, met with his father, Mir Hussain Ali, and assured the family that they would be provided complete justice. Talking to the media after the meeting, Lanjar had said a decision had been taken to conduct a judicial inquiry, under the supervision of a Sindh High Court judge, into the murder case. However, Jibran Nasir, the family’s lawyer, posted on X that they had not requested or consented to any judicial commission. “Nor do we believe it’s required at this stage. A new investigation team has been formed, which the family will meet tomorrow. The Sindh government should not try to create hurdles/confusion in the name of ‘facilitation,’“ he said. He had earlier also objected to the initially constituted police team probing the case and demanded that it be replaced. Speaking to the media on Saturday after the results of the second autopsy came out, he had said that he and the family had “no faith” in the investigation team. Subsequently, the Sindh inspector general of police’s office notified on Sunday the reconstitution of the investigating team probing the case. The order to this effect said the new investigation team was formed in light of Ali’s second postmortem report, which contradicted the one released after his first postmortem. The same day, Karachi police chief Azad Khan also suspended Sharea Faisal Sub-divisional Police Officer (SDPO) Muhammad Arshad Afridi and Gulistan-i-Jauhar Station House Officer (SHO) Kamran Qureshi with immediate effect for failing to preserve the crime scene and conduct a proper crime-scene investigation after Ali’s body was found. The city police chief also ordered the case be transferred to Zaman Town Police Station from Ferozabad Police Station, where the case was initially registered. Controversy over autopsy The latest developments in the case follow a controversy between the Karachi police surgeon and investigators over alleged loopholes in the medico-legal report regarding Ali’s first post-mortem examination. Karachi Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed told a private news channel last week that the post-mortem findings of Ali’s body had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. The police surgeon, whose assessment was based only on the post-mortem report and photographs as she had not examined the body herself back then, had said the reported entry wound, bullet trajectory and exit wound did not correspond with one another. The police surgeon noted that entry wounds were typically smaller than exit wounds in firearm cases. She also said that gunshot residue, commonly found on the hands in suspected suicides, was not tested for in this case. Her interview prompted the police authorities to issue a statement, terming such observations as having the potential to adversely affect the ongoing investigation. The statement, however, said that exhumation of the body could be done on the medical board’s recommendation for further clarification by a committee of medico-legal experts with the court’s permission. On August 6, a judicial magistrate had allowed the exhumation of the body on an application filed by Ali’s father, directing the police surgeon and the Sindh health secretary to constitute a medical board for the exhumation. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with Dr Syed as the convener. However, in the early hours of August 7, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed. But Ali’s family rejected the new board, which also resulted in the deferment of the planned exhumation on Friday. Meanwhile, Nasir accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts. The Sindh government then restored the original medical board, following which Ali’s body was exhumed on Saturday. After a second postmortem of the body, Dr Syed told Dawn that multiple injuries were found on the head and face. “Fractured rib on the back, which is the entry wound of the gunshot [that] exited from the front,” she said. She said the body bore “injuries in the right flank and feet [and] congealed black substance present in the mouth and throat”.

items.title: Man arrested after boat capsizes near Statue of Liberty killing woman and infant
items.description: The operator of a boat that overturned near the Statue of Liberty, killing a woman and a baby,has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment, New York police said. Officials said a large search and rescue operation was launched after the incident near New York Harbour on Saturday night. Twelve people who were initially rescued from the water are all reported to be in stable condition. New York police divers later found a 27-year-old woman and a five-month-old girl, who were transported to a nearby hospital where they later died. The names of passengers and the specific cause of the incident have not been released by officials. While officials have not publicly named the two victims, co-workers of the woman who died have done so. Law enforcement sources who spoke to CBS News, the BBC’s US partner, made the same identification. The New York restaurant Il Punto Ristorante said on social media that the two victims, Sara Sanchez and her baby Antonella Garcia, were the wife and child of one of their employees, Andres Garcia, who was on the boat as well when it overturned. “What was meant to be a joyful family outing ended in unimaginable tragedy,” the restaurant wrote on Instagram. Around 22:25 local time (02:25 GMT), police received a 911 call reporting an overturned boat in the waters near Liberty Island, which houses the iconic statue. A nearby tour operator Sea the City saw the capsized boat and helped pull 11 people from the water, the company’s founder Adam Schwartz said, according to CBS. The rescue involved two US Coast Guard (USCG) boats, four fire department boats, two police boats and a police helicopter, the USCG said. The investigation into the incident is ongoing, officials said. The boat’s operator, a 46-year-old Manhattan resident, faces 13 counts of reckless endangerment, officials said. He has been identified as Manuel Hernandez, according to US media including CBS. Coast Guard investigators are also determining whether the boat was illegally chartered. An illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that does not have required credentials, safety equipment, and certificate of inspection. “We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessel who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water,” said Capt Doreen McCarthy of the USCG.

items.title: 2027 Hajj: Sokoto begins early seat sales as Saudi deadline looms
items.description: …Initial fare put at N7.7m By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto SOKOTO — The Sokoto State Pilgrims Welfare Agency (PWA) has commenced the early sale of seats for the 2027 Hajj, urging intending pilgrims to secure their slots ahead of the deadline set by the Saudi Arabian authorities. The move is aimed at giving prospective pilgrims adequate time to make preparations for the pilgrimage while enabling the state to meet requirements stipulated by the Saudi authorities and the National Hajj Commission of Nigeria (NAHCON). Chairman of the Sokoto State Pilgrims Welfare Agency, Alhaji Aliyu Musa, disclosed that the state had been allocated 2,723 seats for the 2027 Hajj. Musa said the early commencement of the sale was designed to prevent last-minute pressure, facilitate proper planning and safeguard the interests of pilgrims from the state. He said the Saudi authorities had fixed September 26 as the deadline for intending pilgrims from Nigeria to complete payment of their Hajj fares, making early registration and payment necessary. According to him, the initial Hajj fare has been fixed at N7.7 million, although the amount remains tentative and could be reviewed depending on the final costs of accommodation, transportation, feeding and other services. The chairman urged intending pilgrims to take advantage of the early commencement of the exercise rather than wait until the deadline approaches. He also warned that payments must be made personally by the intending pilgrims and not through proxies, stressing that all transactions must comply with procedures prescribed by the agency. Musa said the measure was intended to promote transparency, accountability and proper documentation while preventing irregularities in the registration and payment process. He assured prospective pilgrims of the commitment of the Sokoto State Government to ensuring a smooth and well-organised 2027 Hajj operation. According to him, the government would continue to support the Pilgrims Welfare Agency in carrying out its responsibilities and providing pilgrims with necessary welfare services and guidance throughout the pilgrimage. Musa also cited the agency’s performance record, saying it had received recognition from the National Hajj Commission of Nigeria (NAHCON), through Hajj reporters, as one of the best-performing pilgrims welfare agencies in the country. He said the recognition had encouraged the agency to sustain and improve its service delivery and pilgrims’ welfare. The chairman advised intending pilgrims to obtain accurate information directly from the agency and complete their registration and payment within the stipulated period. He described the early commencement of the seat sales as a deliberate strategy to ensure that Sokoto pilgrims were adequately prepared and able to meet all relevant deadlines. “The objective is to start early, plan properly and avoid the difficulties associated with last-minute arrangements,” he said. The post 2027 Hajj: Sokoto begins early seat sales as Saudi deadline looms appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Vo/Culture : La 1ère édition de la fête traditionnelle « Zootilanyoza » célébrée à Zooti-Centre
items.description: Vogan, 10 août (ATOP) – Les natifs des villages du Grand Zooti ont célébré dans l’allégresse, la 1 ère édition de leur fête traditionnelle « Zootilanyoza », le samedi 8 août, à Zooti-Centre dans la commune Vo 3. Placée sous le signe de l’union et du développement, la célébration de « Zootilanyoza » vise à préserver l’identité culturelle et à renforcer la fraternité entre les filles et fils du milieu. Il s’agit également de rendre hommage aux ancêtres pour les valeurs de solidarité, de respect, de paix, transmis aux générations puis de réfléchir sur le développement du Grand Zooti. La célébration a réuni les populations des 6 villages de Zooti à savoir : Zooti-Glopé, Zooti-Attitedomé, Zooti-Atsanvé, Zooti-Centre, Zooti-Kouessankondji et Zooti-Soko. Des sénateurs, députés, des autorités traditionnelles, administratives, militaires, des conseillers municipaux, des délégations de la diaspora et d’autres préfectures y ont également pris part. La manifestation a été marquée par des opérations de salubrité, des rencontres sportives, des animations culturelles et des causeries-débats. Elle a été aussi meublée par la prestation de différents groupes folkloriques et la remise de trophées aux anciens et nouveaux chefs traditionnels ainsi que celle des médailles aux acteurs de développement de la localité. Remise de trophée à un chef de village par le maire Kloutse (à droite) Le maire de Vo 3, Kloutsè Yao Elom a invité la population à préserver l’unité, la cohésion, et le vivre ensemble afin que la deuxième édition fasse voir les fruits du développement issus de leur participation. Il a sollicité des garants des us et coutumes des prières pour tous les fils de la préfecture, et demandé à la population de participer activement au développement de la commune. Le chef du village de Zooti centre, Togbui Yawo Kpomayizoun Tonou IV a indiqué que cette fête est axée sur l’inspiration selon lequel « seul on va plus vite mais, ensemble on va plus loin ». Il a invité la population à la cohésion sociale que prône la politique nationale et à des actions de développement pour faire du Grand Zooti, une cité rurale. Le président du comité d’organisation, Tonou Francis a convié toute la population à faire de ses différences, une source de richesse et à se sentir concerné par le développement du milieu. Il a invité les jeunes à être des bâtisseurs et des gardiens de la culture. ATOP/AKS /BA/BV

items.title: Battle for Mali base has killed dozens of militants, army says
items.description: The authorities in Mali say their soldiers killed dozens of militant Islamists as they repelled an attack on a military base on Sunday. Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), a jihadist group affiliated to al-Qaeda, said it was behind the assault where its fighters took control of the base in the town of San. The army, which also suffered casualties, disputed it had ceded control – but said its soldiers had to “retreat temporarily”. It comes as Mali’s security situation appears to be deteriorating, more than a decade after a jihadist insurgency began taking root in the north of the country. “The enemy was eliminated and the attack was successfully repelled. Around 40 terrorists were eliminated,” Lt Col El Oumrani, the commander of the 23rd regiment in the San garrison, said in a video. He urged residents to remain vigilant, insisting that his soldiers had “not gone anywhere” and the base remained under army control. “The camp of the 23rd is not empty, it is under the custody of the army.” The attack started at around 05:00 local time (GMT) on Sunday and lasted for about two hours, according to witnesses quoted by the French broadcaster RFI. The attackers came on motorcycles and on foot, some disguised in army uniforms to infiltrate the base, RFI reported the witnesses as saying. One said the militants entered the camp and held it “for a long time before leaving”. “I noticed that the fighting took place between 200 and 300 metres from the camp. Several terrorists were killed by soldiers, but others fled; some even hid in houses and others went into the forest,” the witness said. At least 10 soldiers were killed in the fighting and the assailants briefly took over the camp, the AFP news agency quoted security and local sources. The army told national broadcaster ORTM that the militants used drones, heavy machine guns and armoured vehicles to breach the site’s perimeter. Since 2012, Mali has been plagued by insurgencies and large parts of the north and east of the country remain outside government control. April saw nationwide, co-ordinated attacks by an alliance of jihadists and separatist rebels in the north – the Azawad Liberation Front – seeking to overthrow the military regime of Gen Assimi Goïta, who seized power in a coup in 2020. During the attacks, Defence Minister Sadio Camara was killed in an apparent suicide truck bombing on his residence near the capital, Bamako. JNIM has diversified its operations and begun targeting not only northern Mali but also central and southern Mali, showing an ability to penetrate deeper into the territory despite numerous military operations. In the wake of the coup, which was in part carried out over the failure to ease the security situation, Mali rejected French military help and instead turned to Russia.

items.title: Pak-Saudi-Turkiye defence pact ‘entirely for defensive purposes’, not aggression: PM Shehbaz
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Monday affirmed that the recently signed Makkah Joint Defence Agreement was “entirely for defensive purposes”, and not for any aggression. The joint defence agreement, signed on August 7 between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empowers its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. Addressing the federal cabinet on Monday, PM Shehbaz recalled that he, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan signed the pact in Makkah on Friday. The prime minister stressed that the objective of the pact is to “promote peace, progress, and prosperity in the region”. “Its purpose is definitely not that any aggression occurs. It is entirely for defensive purposes, for peace, tranquillity and progress in the region,” he affirmed. “I believe this agreement is a source of strength not just among these three countries, but for the entire Muslim ummah,” he noted. PM Shehbaz particularly felicitated Deputy PM and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar as well as Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) Field Marshal Asim Munir on the signing of the agreement. Efforts for the joint defence pact had been underway for “many years and materialised this Friday”, the prime minister said. He noted that while Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had already entered the “ Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement ” in September 2025, Islamabad and Ankara also had “arrangements for decades” between them. PM Shehbaz recalled that the Pakistani nation and the army had been honoured to “defend the world’s holiest places” of Makkah and Madina for years along with the Saudi forces. “Last year, with Allah’s grace, this arrangement was officially recognised so that a proper agreement was signed. Friday’s agreement is another extension of it, with a trilateral agreement signed.” In a statement issued by the Foreign Office earlier in the day, Dar felicitated the nation on the agreement’s signing. He reiterated his comments from Sunday wherein he said the pact was defensive in nature and not directed against any country. Dar also noted that the term of treating an attack on one of them as an attack against all three was “consistent with the inherent right of individual and collective self-defence under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter”. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement has been hailed by the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) as an “important strategic step”. Kuwait , Bahrain and Somalia are among the countries that have welcomed it. Iran’s comments also took a rather positive tone, stressing its stance of pursuing “security mechanisms based on cooperation between regional countries”. More to follow

items.title: 33 girls rescued from trafficking, forced to pay up to GH¢20,000 for freedom
items.description: Thirty-three girls and young women have been rescued from trafficking and sexual exploitation in a weekend operation, with survivors telling investigators they were allegedly made to pay up to GH¢20,000 to secure their freedom. The operation was led by the Anti-Human Trafficking Unit (AHTU) of the Ghana Police Service, with support from child rights organisation Challenging Heights. The survivors are currently receiving care, including medical attention, psychosocial support and shelter from the organisation. Challenging Heights said some of those rescued are believed to be children, although several have been reluctant to disclose their ages because of the trauma and coercion they have experienced. According to Challenging Heights, testimonies gathered from the survivors point to an organised commercial operation involving recruitment, transportation, supervision, financial targets and punishment. President of the organisation, Dr James Kofi Annan , said the accounts have raised fresh concerns about the scale and sophistication of trafficking networks operating across borders. “These girls paid their own way into Ghana and were then told to pay again for their own freedom. A young woman who is told she must pay GH¢20,000 to redeem her freedom. You are certainly selling her back to herself,” he said. He warned that rescuing victims without dismantling the networks behind their exploitation could result in others being brought in to replace them. “Thirty-three girls came out this weekend, and unless we reach the people at the top of this chain, all thirty-three will simply be replaced,” Dr Annan added. Challenging Heights said the survivors reported paying their own transport and travel expenses, including money given to people who facilitated their journeys. Upon arrival in Ghana, however, they were allegedly told they owed additional amounts—reaching as much as GH¢20,000—to secure their release. The organisation said the women were allegedly compelled to engage in commercial sex to raise the money, with their earnings taken from them and daily financial targets imposed. Challenging Heights says the accounts point to a trafficking network involving several specialised roles, including recruiters, transporters and individuals who allegedly supervise victims after their arrival. The organisation also alleged that some immigration officials may have been compromised, a claim that would require investigation and verification by the relevant authorities. It is therefore calling for stronger investigative and prosecutorial capacity to enable Ghanaian authorities to identify and prosecute those behind such networks. The organisation also wants dedicated human trafficking courts established without further delay. It welcomed an earlier announcement by Chief Justice Justice Paul Baffoe-Bonnie about plans to introduce specialised courts for cases including human trafficking and cross-border crime. Challenging Heights is now calling for a clear implementation timetable and specialised training for judges handling trafficking and trauma-related cases. The organisation is also demanding increased personnel and resources for the AHTU, the Ghana Immigration Service and specialised prosecution teams. It wants investigators equipped with financial investigation and asset-tracing capabilities, digital forensic tools, online recruitment analysis and stronger intelligence-sharing mechanisms with Nigerian authorities. Challenging Heights cited official figures showing that Ghana recorded 273 human trafficking investigations, 65 prosecutions and 25 convictions in 2024. The organisation argues that while Ghana has legislation criminalising trafficking, the scale and sophistication of the networks require greater institutional capacity to identify perpetrators and follow the money behind the trade. It is also calling for specialised, trauma-informed training for investigators and prosecutors and for any official complicity uncovered through investigations to be prosecuted. The latest operation follows other interventions supported by Challenging Heights in 2026. The organisation said it supported the rescue of 144 victims of trafficking and modern slavery during the first half of the year , including 42 children rescued from forced labour on Lake Volta and 102 Nigerian nationals. It has also previously called for investigations into allegations of a cross-border baby-harvesting and baby-selling network based on accounts from survivors. Challenging Heights stressed at the time that those allegations had not been independently verified but said the accounts were serious enough to warrant investigation. Challenging Heights said it is ready to work with the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Human Trafficking Secretariat, Ghana Police Service, Ghana Immigration Service and Judicial Service, alongside civil society organisations, to combat trafficking. The organisation has previously called for at least GH¢20 million to be allocated to agencies responsible for preventing, investigating and prosecuting trafficking. It says sustained investment in victim protection, investigations and prosecutions will be necessary to dismantle trafficking networks and prevent rescued victims from being replaced by others. Over the past two decades, Challenging Heights says it has supported the rescue of nearly 3,000 children and young people from trafficking and exploitation, alongside rehabilitation, reintegration and livelihood support.

items.title: Our tourism minister has failed – Austine Woode
items.description: Ghanaian broadcaster Austine Woode has expressed his disappointment about the performance of the Minister of Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts, Abla Dzifa Gomashie. Speaking during the ninth edition of Joy FM’s Showbiz Roundtable on Saturday, 8th August 2026, Austine said the minister had not laid down plans that would impact the industry in reality. Austine said the minister had been more focused on holding workshops and stakeholder engagements than getting on the ground to keep things running. “I have a problem with our minister. She is from our stock but she has failed for me. I am from Kumasi, has she spoken to anybody about the land on which they will build the Kumasi theatre? I am a stakeholder there. If she had had any conversation like that, I would know that they are looking for the land. They are not doing it,” he said. “What they are doing is throwing things against the wall and the one that will stick, they come and highlight it. All of those things are not going to help the people. Let us go to the basics and build from there. When we build from there, all the industry will enjoy from it; not what they are doing. They have failed,” he added. Austine Woode In line with his concerns, the President of the Foundation of Concerned Arts Professionals (FOCAP) also said his group would score the current government 0%. However, the Minister said during the Government Accountability Series on Monday, 10th August 2026, that after a tour of the Ashanti Region, she noticed that there were infrastructural projects that needed completion. She said she had therefore suggested that those facilities be completed rather than starting a new theatre. Themed “Assessing 20 Months of Government’s Impact on Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts”, the ninth Showbiz Roundtable examined the government’s commitments to the sector, assessed the level of implementation, measured the impact of policies and explored the road ahead for Ghana’s creative economy. The discussion featured industry figures including Chief Operating Officer of Maestro Africa Group, Francis Doku; Lead Consultant at Jesse Agyepong and Associates, Jesse Agyepong; pop culture journalist Olele Salvador; and Joy FM broadcaster Ken Addy. Also in attendance were comedians Lekzy DeComic, Kojo Pjay, Percy Obrempong, James Brown and Jacinta. Others were broadcasters Austine Woode and Kojo Preko Dankwah, while tourism professional Emmanuel Frimpong was also present. The discussion was moderated by broadcaster and arts and culture journalist Kwame Dadzie. It was produced by Philip Nai, with support from Anita Teye and Idah Lamaire.

items.title: Europe braces for another summer heatwave
items.description: Much of Europe is bracing for yet another heatwave following periods of scorching temperatures that have driven rivers to record lows, ignited historic forest fires and contributed to thousands of deaths. Parts of Britain and France on Monday were already under extreme heat warnings with forecasts of temperatures around the mid-30s Celsius. Unusually high temperatures were also forecast in coming days across a swathe of countries not accustomed to the heat, such as Switzerland, Austria and Hungary. Europe’s weather warning system MeteoAlarm on Monday said scorching temperatures are already being felt across much of Italy and coastal areas of Croatia. Here’s what to know as temperatures soar again across the continent, the fastest-warming on the planet due to human-caused climate change. ‘Intense heat’ The United Kingdom’s Met Office warned at the weekend that the summer’s fifth hot spell was about to take hold in a country whose infrastructure has been built for a more temperate, cooler climate. “Yet another spell of extremely hot weather is set to spread north across much of the UK with temperatures reaching the mid-30s Celsius in places,” it said on X on Sunday. Half of England and the whole of Wales is already officially in drought — leaving 23 million people subject to hosepipe bans — with more English regions expected to be declared in drought later Monday. Next to no rain was in forecasts for impacted areas this week. In France, the national weather agency Meteo-France warned on Monday that the southeast would see temperatures as high as 35°C, with that level of spreading as the week progresses. “The intense heat will affect almost the entire country between Wednesday and Friday,” it said in a bulletin. The agency also warned that due to climate change, “future summers will generally be hotter than those experienced to date”. Both France and the UK have seen thousands of excess deaths during previous heatwaves this year. Fires and drought Greece reported its second fire this season to spark near the capital Athens on Monday, dispatching hundreds of crew and equipment. Already, more than 10,000 hectares of pine forests were blackened by a blaze that broke out 10 days ago northwest of the capital. France and Spain have already seen historic wildfires so far this summer, with record levels of drought causing tinder-dry conditions. Heat and drought are also driving rivers across Europe to record lows. The Rhine in Germany could drop so much it becomes unnavigable, industry groups warned Monday. Cargo ships have managed to continue transporting goods along the river, which flows through the industrial heartland of Europe’s top economy, but with reduced loads and at higher costs. And Polish officials announced that the Vistula, the country’s longest river, had matched its record low in Warsaw on Monday — a record only set on Friday. Low levels along the Danube river have already forced Hungary and Romania to shutter its nuclear plants, which rely on the water for cooling, since late July. By the numbers Nearly 120 million Europeans live in regions where July 2026 was the hottest ever recorded, according to an AFP analysis of national weather agencies and Copernicus climate data. The records were concentrated in southern Britain, western France, and northern and eastern Spain. At least 12,000 excess deaths were recorded across nine European countries during one heatwave in June, an AFP analysis of national statistics found last month, a toll that could rise as more data is released. Solar eclipse A solar eclipse occurring on Wednesday that will be visible across parts of the European continent is expected to attract skygazers despite the unwelcoming weather. The European Space Agency’s observatory in Teruel, Spain, will host a day of activities up to the main event with the eclipse beginning at 7:33pm CEST (10:33pm PKT) and reaching totality at 8:23pm. The area saw temperatures breach 30°C on Monday, and the eclipse will cross over areas that were hit by the devastating Spanish fires last month.

items.title: Forum humanitaire de l’AES: à la recherche d’un modèle sahélien fondé sur la souveraineté et la résilience
items.description: Le Premier ministre, le Camarade Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a présidé, ce lundi 10 août 2026 à Ouagadougou, la cérémonie d’ouverture de la deuxième édition du Forum humanitaire de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES), couplée à la deuxième réunion des ministres chargés du Genre de l’espace confédéral. Réunissant des délégations du Burkina Faso, du Mali et du Niger, ces deux rencontres traduisent la volonté des États membres de renforcer leur coopération face aux défis humanitaires, tout en accordant une place centrale à la résilience des communautés et à l’autonomisation des femmes. À l’ouverture des travaux, le Chef du Gouvernement a rendu hommage à la vision et au leadership des Chefs d’État de l’espace confédéral, engagés dans la consolidation d’une souveraineté fondée sur les réalités et les aspirations des peuples du Sahel. Le couplage du Forum humanitaire avec la réunion des ministres chargés du Genre s’inscrit, selon lui, dans cette dynamique et traduit une approche intégrée associant action humanitaire, relèvement, résilience, inclusion sociale et égalité de genre. Le deuxième Forum humanitaire est placé sous le thème : « De l’urgence à la résilience : vers un modèle d’action humanitaire intégré pour l’AES ». La deuxième réunion des ministres chargés du Genre porte, pour sa part, sur le thème : « Mise en œuvre des référentiels nationaux de développement des pays de l’AES : contribution des femmes à la construction d’un espace souverain, résilient et prospère ». Ces réflexions interviennent dans un contexte marqué par des défis sécuritaires, humanitaires, climatiques et économiques qui aggravent les vulnérabilités et affectent durement les populations, notamment les plus fragiles. Face à cette situation, le Camarade Premier ministre a salué la détermination des peuples et des forces armées des pays de l’AES engagés dans la reconquête du territoire. Pour lui, cette dynamique de souveraineté ne peut toutefois se limiter au domaine sécuritaire. Elle doit aussi se traduire par la capacité des États à définir leurs priorités et à conduire leurs propres politiques de développement. Cette exigence suppose de repenser en profondeur l’action humanitaire afin qu’elle ne se limite plus à la seule gestion de l’urgence, mais contribue également au renforcement des capacités nationales, locales et communautaires. « L’assistance ne saurait être une finalité en soi. L’action humanitaire doit répondre à l’urgence tout en préparant les conditions de l’autonomie », a déclaré le Chef du Gouvernement. Le Premier ministre a ainsi plaidé pour une meilleure articulation entre action humanitaire, relèvement et développement, dans le respect de la souveraineté des États, de la dignité des populations, du leadership des autorités nationales et des principes humanitaires. La réflexion engagée à Ouagadougou s’inscrit dans la continuité de la première édition du Forum, organisée à Bamako en 2025, qui avait permis de poser les bases d’une coopération renforcée, notamment en matière de coordination et de financement de l’action humanitaire. Accueillie par le Burkina Faso dans le cadre de sa présidence de la Confédération, cette deuxième édition doit permettre d’aller plus loin dans la consolidation de ces acquis. Les échanges portent notamment sur le renforcement de la gouvernance et de la coordination humanitaires, la mutualisation des capacités, le partage d’expériences, la préparation aux crises et la mobilisation de ressources endogènes. Ils doivent aussi permettre d’approfondir les réflexions sur la prévention, l’alerte précoce, le relèvement socio-économique, la restauration des moyens d’existence et la réhabilitation des services sociaux de base. Le Chef du Gouvernement a, dans le même esprit, appelé à des mécanismes de financement plus prévisibles et davantage endogènes, ainsi qu’à une amélioration du ciblage, de la coordination et de la redevabilité de l’action humanitaire. La construction de ce modèle plus autonome et plus résilient repose également sur une meilleure valorisation de la contribution des femmes. Le Camarade Premier ministre a rappelé leur rôle central dans la cohésion sociale, les activités productives, l’éducation, la prévention des conflits et la reconstruction du tissu communautaire. La deuxième réunion des ministres chargés du Genre devra notamment faire le bilan de la mise en œuvre de la feuille de route sur la Déclaration de Niamey, identifier des mécanismes de financement endogènes et innovants, procéder au lancement officiel de la plateforme régionale des organisations de femmes de l’AES et formuler des recommandations pour renforcer leur participation au développement de l’espace confédéral. Pour le Premier ministre, la construction d’une Confédération forte et résiliente passe nécessairement par une pleine reconnaissance de la contribution des femmes et par leur participation effective aux instances de décision, aux politiques publiques ainsi qu’à la vie économique et sociale. Tout en saluant l’engagement des acteurs humanitaires nationaux, communautaires et internationaux, il a insisté sur la nécessité d’une réponse durable, alignée sur les priorités définies par les États et orientée vers le relèvement et l’autonomie des communautés. « Ensemble, nous avons la responsabilité historique de faire émerger, à partir de nos réalités, un modèle humanitaire sahélien, porté par les États, ancré dans les communautés et centré sur les populations », a-t-il déclaré. Dans son intervention, le Coordonnateur résident et Coordonnateur humanitaire des Nations Unies au Burkina Faso, M. Njoya Tikum, a salué la dynamique engagée par les États de l’AES et l’évolution vers une action humanitaire davantage orientée vers la résilience et le développement durable. Il a indiqué que « le système des Nations Unies partage pleinement la direction fixée par ce forum » et réaffirmé sa disponibilité à accompagner le Burkina Faso, le Mali et le Niger dans la mise en œuvre des recommandations, dans un esprit de respect, de dialogue et de partenariat. M. Njoya Tikum a également insisté sur la nécessité d’adapter les réponses humanitaires aux réalités de chaque territoire et de renforcer les capacités nationales et locales. « Notre rôle n’est pas de prendre la place de ceux qui sont aux premières lignes. Notre rôle est de renforcer les capacités et de les soutenir », a-t-il souligné. À travers le Forum de Ouagadougou, les États membres entendent ainsi consolider leur coopération et faire émerger des réponses communes, durables et adaptées aux réalités des populations sahéliennes. DCRP/Primature L’article Forum humanitaire de l’AES: à la recherche d'un modèle sahélien fondé sur la souveraineté et la résilience est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

CSOs demand probe into 2022 AKSA Energy agreement renewal after US bribery conviction
items.description: Civil society organisations are demanding an immediate review and investigation into the circumstances surrounding the renewal of the AKSA Energy agreement with the government of Ghana in October 2022. The groups say the manner in which the agreement was renewed raises serious questions about transparency, accountability and whether the transaction was conducted in the national interest. Their concerns have resurfaced following the conviction of former Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) Managing Director, Asante Kwaku Berko, by a United States court for bribing government officials in connection with a power plant deal involving Ghana in 2015. The conviction has renewed scrutiny of the circumstances surrounding the power deal and the possible involvement of public officials. Vice-President of IMANI Africa, Kofi Bentil, is demanding the immediate arrest and investigation of officials implicated in the scandal. “The officials implicated in the scandal must be immediately arrested and investigations initiated,” he said. He questioned why Ghanaian authorities had not acted decisively despite information emerging from the US proceedings. “We who suffered, we whose citizens die, we whose economy is ground to a halt, sat and watched politicians make money off our backs as people die,” he said. Mr Bentil argued that the President, the police and the Attorney General have the authority to initiate investigations into the individuals named in connection with the bribery scheme. “Nothing stops the OSP tomorrow. Nothing stops EOCO tomorrow and nothing stops the Attorney General tomorrow from telling them to do so, to tell us what we did and what you are going to do with this information,” he added. Also, Chairman of the AU Advisory Board Against Corruption, Edem Senanu, has also raised concerns about Ghana’s ability to detect and investigate corruption involving public officials. He expressed concern that the alleged transactions could have taken place without adequate scrutiny from Ghanaian institutions. “I am really embarrassed that any Ghanaian within that system should think that you just be giving money to be paying these things and there was not going to be any cross-checking,” he said. According to him, the discovery of crucial information in a private email account highlights the extent to which external investigations may sometimes uncover wrongdoing that domestic systems fail to detect. He noted that the US authorities were able to identify details of the alleged scheme through their own investigations. Deputy Attorney General Justice Srem-Sai has meanwhile disclosed that the Attorney General is working with US authorities to bring persons implicated in the alleged bribery scheme to book. In a post on Facebook, he said Ghanaian authorities were engaging their American counterparts as investigations into the matter continue. The latest demands follow Asante Kwaku Berko’s conviction by a United States federal jury in Brooklyn, New York, on charges of conspiracy to violate the United States’ Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and other related laws. The development brings renewed attention to the controversial power plant contract and the alleged corruption surrounding its development between 2014 and 2017. The civil society groups insist that the conviction in the United States provides sufficient grounds for Ghanaian authorities to reopen questions surrounding the transaction and establish whether any Ghanaian officials breached the law or abused public office.

items.title: Ofori-Atta trial set to resume August 27 after Supreme Court clears OSP Act
items.description: The criminal trial of former Finance Minister Ken Ofori-Atta is expected to resume on Thursday, August 27, 2026, following a Supreme Court decision upholding the constitutional validity of the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP) Act, 2017 (Act 959). The OSP announced the date in a Facebook post on Monday, August 10, signalling the return of proceedings in a number of corruption cases that had been placed on hold since April this year. The Supreme Court ruling effectively removes a major legal hurdle that had raised questions about the OSP’s authority to investigate and prosecute corruption-related offences without prior authorisation. The suspension of proceedings followed an earlier High Court decision that questioned aspects of the OSP’s prosecutorial mandate. 28 counts against Ofori-Atta Mr Ofori-Atta is standing trial on 28 counts of corruption and corruption-related offences arising from the OSP’s investigation into revenue assurance contracts between Strategic Mobilisation Limited (SML) and the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA). The former minister was initially charged together with seven other persons on 78 counts in November 2025. The charges were subsequently amended, resulting in Mr Ofori-Atta facing 28 counts, while the other accused persons face separate charges linked to the case. Those also before the court include former GRA Commissioners-General Emmanuel Kofi Nti and Ammishaddai Owusu-Amoah; former Customs Commissioners Isaac Crentsil and Kwadwo Damoah; SML Chief Executive Officer Evans Adusei; and former Chief of Cabinet to Mr Ofori-Atta, Ernest Darko Akore. The prosecution alleges that the accused persons were involved in various acts of corruption and corruption-related offences connected with the SML-GRA revenue assurance arrangements. The case has attracted considerable public interest because of the financial implications of the contracts and the roles allegedly played by officials and private-sector actors in their implementation. Ofori-Atta’s US residency The former Finance Minister has also secured permanent residency in the United States after a US Immigration Court approved his application for adjustment of status. His lawyers announced in June 2026 that his application for a Green Card had been approved following immigration proceedings concerning his status in the United States. The development, however, has been the subject of public discussion in Ghana, particularly because the OSP has been pursuing steps connected with his return to Ghana to face the criminal proceedings. The OSP has rejected suggestions that the US immigration decision constituted a finding on the merits of the corruption case against Mr Ofori-Atta. The anti-corruption agency explained that it was not a party to the US immigration proceedings and that its involvement in the United States relates to extradition proceedings being pursued through the Attorney-General. It further clarified that the extradition documents were not before the US Immigration Court. The OSP has consequently cautioned against treating findings made in the immigration proceedings as a determination of the credibility of the evidence or allegations underpinning the criminal case in Ghana. With the Supreme Court having now upheld the OSP Act, attention is expected to shift to the resumption of the substantive proceedings against Mr Ofori-Atta and the other accused persons.

items.title: Power up: How EU-Africa cooperation can drive Europe’s battery recycling future
items.description: Cover image: picture alliance / NTB | Fredrik Varfjell Recycling is no longer just an environmental obligation. It has become a geoeconomic imperative directly linked to Europe’s energy security and industrial competitiveness. The European Commission’s Critical Raw Materials Act reflects this change—it has set an ambitious target to source at least 25% of the EU’s annual consumption of strategic raw materials from recycling by 2030. Europe, however, is making little progress. A recent European Court of Auditors’ report suggests that seven of 26 energy-transition-related minerals have recycling rates between 1% and 5% in the EU. This means, for example, that Europe is recovering just three tonnes from every 100 tonnes of natural graphite contained in batteries. According to the report, there are another ten minerals that Europe does not recycle at all, including lithium, gallium and silicon metal. As such, recycling battery materials warrants far more attention. This valuable source of critical minerals could lower the continent’s dependence on Chinese mineral value chains; recycling battery materials is also much quicker than relying on the development of mines elsewhere that produce the same materials. However, fragmentation, red tape and unfavourable economics are hampering Europe’s recycling efforts, in part due to a regulatory framework that still treats battery materials as hazardous waste rather than a source of strategically important minerals. Europeans need to focus on battery materials regulation with an industrial policy lens and pursue strategic partnerships with African countries to make gains in material recovery. Using black mass and EVs Recovered minerals from Europe’s waste—including end-of-life electric vehicle (EV) batteries, wind turbines, industrial parts and electrical wiring—are insufficient to meet all of Europe’s mineral needs. However, they can substitute for a share of primary minerals from mining, which would help Europeans derisk from Chinese mineral supply chains far quicker than new mines can come into production. Europe will have relatively significant EV battery feedstock for recycling in coming years. Europeans were early adopters of EVs and European countries are global leaders in terms of EV sales as a share of total car sales: in Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands, for example, EVs account for 58%, 56% and 48% of passenger-vehicle sales respectively, while fully electric vehicles comprise 22.6% of cars registered in the EU. High EV adoption means Europe should have a solid supply of EV battery feedstock for recycling facilities, provided it keeps this within the EU for recycling. In March 2025, the EU re-classified “black mass” (the shredded EV battery waste processed to recover critical minerals) and end-of-life lithium-based, nickel-based and zinc-based batteries as “ hazardous waste ”. Black mass is important because it contains valuable critical minerals; if Europeans can process this within its borders, it can feed recovered minerals into European industry. This new classification prohibits export of black mass to non-OECD countries, while requiring that shipments within the EU and the OECD have prior notification and consent from the import, export and transit countries involved. Europe currently exports around 80% of its black mass for refining elsewhere, mostly in Asia; South Korea’s OECD status and cheap recycling capacities make it a key destination, for example. The reclassification of black mass raises bureaucratic barriers to exporting out of the EU, contributing to efforts to prevent recycling feedstock leaking out. However, black mass is now more difficult to move within Europe, too, which makes aggregating feedstock for recycling within the EU a challenge. While Europe has some battery shredding (or pre-treatment) capacity to produce black mass, its refining capacity to recover minerals from black mass has lagged significantly. Figure 1a Figure 1b Although forecasts suggest that Europe will slightly raise its material-recovery capacity in the coming years, it remains a minor player. China’s dominant share in global battery recycling capacity for the shredding and material recovery stages, which exceeded 80% in 2025, is set to continue. Recent analysis estimates that the costs of hydrometallurgical recycling for nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries are respectively 70% and 67% higher in France than in China due to higher labour, energy, environmental compliance, dismantling and transport costs in Europe. China’s scale of feedstock—domestic supply of end-of-life batteries, scrap metal from the local automobile industry, and imported batteries and black mass—has further lowered their recycling costs. Making battery recycling happen in Europe The EU can take three clear steps to increase recycling black mass in Europe. First, Europeans should implement stricter export restrictions on black mass and batteries to fully close off exports and retain the products for material recovery domestically. [1] The US took this position in July 2026, with President Donald Trump empowering federal officials to block exports of end-of-life batteries and electronic waste to contain these products for recycling within the US. Second, Europeans need to urgently build more recycling capacity to refine black mass: Europe’s hydrometallurgical recycling capacity is less than 3,000 tonnes , which is around one-sixtieth of China’s. Estimates suggest that Europe needs the capacity to recycle 120,000–135,000 tonnes of black mass per year by 2030. Third—and perhaps most challenging—Europeans need to ensure recycling in Europe becomes more economically viable. Failing this, tough export restrictions will lead to battery waste being stockpiled rather than recycled. To achieve the above, Europeans need to develop new financing mechanisms—such as building recycling costs into the purchase price of products and using public finance to help offset recyclers’ higher costs in Europe—to make recycling more economically viable. This would be particularly timely as battery technology shifts from NMC to LFP batteries: since the latter are comprised of less valuable minerals, recyclers earn less from the sale of recovered minerals, necessitating support for project viability. The provision of public finance, preferably at both the EU and member-state level, would help in the development of new technologies and processes that lower recycling costs by reducing energy requirements and improving recovery rates. Patent filings in battery recycling are growing significantly, with 2026 figures showing a 103% growth in filings (adjusted for lag). China leads in patent applications, although US and European companies—notably Belgium’s Umicore—are also active. To make Europe more globally competitive in recycling, Europe must increase its investments in innovation using public finance support. Europeans also need to establish a strong domestic value chain. European battery recyclers, such as Germany’s Cylib and Tozero and Norway’s Hydrovolt, should identify and establish commercial agreements with EU-based offtakers for the minerals they recover—after all, if Europe has to export recovered minerals outside its borders for want of domestic offtakers, gains in recycling will be for nothing. Specifically, this requires European industry that uses recovered minerals (alongside primary source minerals from mining) to refine precursor cathode active material (pCAM) and cathode active material (CAM) stages for EV batteries. Pursuing EU-Africa partnerships Europeans should also look internationally to ensure recycling can feasibly reduce existing mineral supply chain dependencies. The EU needs to tap into other recycling feedstock markets and diversify its mineral supply chains by establishing recycling partnerships with OECD and non-OECD countries. Indeed, the EU has explicitly included recycling within the remit of some strategic partnerships on critical minerals that it has signed with partner countries, including several African countries such as Namibia . By locating recycling and mineral-processing facilities in African countries, they can tackle the cost disadvantages Europeans face with regard to energy, land and labour costs on home soil. Namibia and Kenya are ideal partners: both have transport corridors and port infrastructure that make them well positioned to aggregate regional battery and electronic waste (e-waste); they can harness their abundant renewable energy resources can power material recovery facilities. EU-Africa cooperation on recycling would also be advantageous to African countries. Joint operations create jobs, expand African mineral processing capabilities and link African mineral supply chains with European industry. Africa-based recycling facilities could also manage the growing quantity of end-of-life batteries and e-waste generated by African countries, notably from solar panels, energy-storage batteries and EV batteries from smaller two- and three-wheeler vehicles. Sub-Saharan Africa’s projected growth in stationary storage capacity alone is significant: following current market trends, it will expand dramatically by 2030, with a storage capacity increase from 11 GWh to 83 GWh. If the region achieves universal access to electricity (SDG7), demand could more than double that, reaching a storage capacity of 190 GWh. Figure 2 Europe’s road ahead More recycling facilities are required to handle Africa’s growing volume of end-of-life battery feedstock. This presents an opportunity for growth both in Africa-based recycling, and in Africa-Europe recycling cooperation. However, this is not straightforward. Africa-Europe recycling partnerships need to invest in formalising supply chains for collection and storage; they need to build facilities for shredding batteries and e-waste; and they need to ensure that they can refine black mass to recover valuable materials. They would also need to develop the workforce skills and local-firm capabilities needed for efficient, environmentally-sound operations throughout the supply chain. For African countries like Namibia and Kenya, such cooperation creates jobs and builds recycling capacity and expertise while integrating African mineral industrialisation into EU mineral supply chains. Recycling operations could also serve as anchor customers for increasing electricity generation and transmission investments in African countries, while local populations also benefit from improved electricity availability. Additionally, recycling in African countries helps address the continent’s growing e-waste management challenges . For Europe, the increased recovery of critical minerals both domestically and through recycling partnerships with African countries offers greater supply chain diversification, access to minerals from non-OECD black mass and de-risking from Chinese mineral supply chains. All of this will happen faster than if Europeans continue to rely on global mine development. Europeans need to extend their strategic thinking beyond their borders, advancing recycling cooperation through critical minerals partnerships. [1] Interview with a representative of a mineral analytics company, February 19th, 2026. Source
